_meta.note: Each trap has real PYQ examples. Use these in blueprint generation to inject specific trap strategies per skeleton.

traps.name: river_lake_wrong_feeder
traps.description: Statement says River X feeds Lake Y — but X only passes through or is adjacent to Y, not the direct feeder. Or the feeder relationship is reversed.
traps.mechanism: Students memorise river names near lakes but not the exact hydrological relationship.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2023: 'Krishna River directly feeds Kolleru Lake' — FALSE. Kolleru lies between Krishna and Godavari deltas but Krishna does not directly feed it. Jhelum passing through Wular Lake was TRUE.
traps.how_to_generate: Pick any Indian lake. Assign the nearest river as the feeder in a false statement. Use actual feeder in correct statement.

traps.name: country_border_length_swap
traps.description: Tests longest/shortest border between two countries — students confuse China-India with Canada-US.
traps.mechanism: Students assume India has long borders since it borders many countries. The Canada-US border is the world's longest, not China-India.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: 'The longest border between any two countries is between China and India' — FALSE. Correct answer: Canada-USA.
traps.how_to_generate: Use superlatives (longest, shortest, highest, deepest) and swap with the second-most-famous answer.

traps.name: sea_ocean_property_reversal
traps.description: Assigns a physical property (precipitation, salinity, no river inflow) to the wrong water body, or reverses a comparative property.
traps.mechanism: Students know properties in isolation but not the correct body they apply to.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024 Red Sea question: Both statements were actually correct — Red Sea has very little precipitation AND no river inflow. Trap was in the options (students expected one to be false).
traps.how_to_generate: State a true property of one sea for a different sea. Or use 'highest salinity' for Red Sea vs Dead Sea confusion.

traps.name: troposphere_thickness_direction_error
traps.description: Reverses the direction of a gradient — e.g., troposphere is thicker at equator vs poles, temperature lapse rates.
traps.mechanism: Students know the concept but flip the direction under exam pressure.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: 'Troposphere is thicker at the equator' — TRUE. Statement II explained it correctly via convectional currents. Trap was making students doubt Statement I because Statement II seemed to explain something they weren't sure about.
traps.how_to_generate: Take any gradient concept (temperature, pressure, thickness, density) and state the correct direction in one statement, reversed in another. Use A/R format.

traps.name: mineral_source_confusion
traps.description: Asks what mineral a rock/ore is a source of — confuses titanium with iron, cobalt with nickel, etc.
traps.mechanism: Students know ore names but not the exact metal extracted from each.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2023: 'Ilmenite and rutile are rich sources of Titanium' — correct. Common trap: students think ilmenite = iron (ilmen = iron in some languages). 2024: DRC cobalt — primary byproduct of copper/nickel mining.
traps.how_to_generate: Give a mineral name + location. Options are 4 metals that are plausibly associated with that region or mineral family.

traps.name: india_vs_china_agricultural_stats
traps.description: Compares India-China on arable land, irrigated area, productivity — two of three stats are true, one flips.
traps.mechanism: India DOES have more arable land and higher irrigation share. But China has HIGHER productivity per hectare. Students assume India beats China on all three.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2023: Three statements about India vs China agriculture — statements 1 and 2 correct, statement 3 (India productivity higher than China) FALSE. Appeared 2+ times in PYQs.
traps.how_to_generate: Use any India vs world comparison (ranks, shares, ratios). Put 2 correct and 1 reversed statement. Make the reversed one the one students are most likely to assume is true.

traps.name: port_classification_first_largest
traps.description: Confuses 'first' (chronologically) with 'largest' — or 'public' with 'private' port classification.
traps.mechanism: Students memorise rankings without understanding classification criteria.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2023: 'Kamarajar Port is first major port registered as a company' — TRUE. 'Mundra Port is largest privately owned' — TRUE. Students failed on the Kamarajar = company registration fact.
traps.how_to_generate: Pick ports/airports/stations. Use superlatives with specific criteria (first by which metric, largest by which measure, greenfield vs brownfield).

traps.name: volcanic_eruption_products
traps.description: Lists volcanic products and asks which are ALL correct — students think nitrogen compounds are NOT volcanic products.
traps.mechanism: Students know lava, ash, sulphur. Nitrogen compounds (NOx) from volcanic eruptions are less memorised.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2023: Pyroclastic debris, ash, nitrogen compounds, sulphur compounds — all four are volcanic products. Answer was 'all of the above' which students avoided.
traps.how_to_generate: Use 'all of the above' as the correct answer when one item seems unlikely. Science-geography overlap questions.

traps.name: tree_type_deciduous_vs_evergreen
traps.description: Classifies trees as deciduous/evergreen — one familiar tree (jackfruit) is evergreen, not deciduous, trapping students.
traps.mechanism: Teak is obviously deciduous. Jackfruit looks like a tropical tree so students assume evergreen — actually it IS evergreen. The trap is Mahua which is also deciduous.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2023: Teak (deciduous), Mahua (deciduous), Jackfruit (evergreen) — answer was 'two are deciduous'.
traps.how_to_generate: Mix trees students know (teak, sal, neem) with less-known ones and ask how many are deciduous/evergreen. Include one that seems counterintuitive.

traps.name: green_field_vs_brown_field_airport
traps.description: Asks which airports are greenfield (built on new land) vs brownfield (expansion of existing) — students assume all new-looking airports are greenfield.
traps.mechanism: Vijayawada airport LOOKS modern but is a very old airport expanded — brownfield. Students assume newness = greenfield.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2023: Donyi Polo (greenfield, correct), Kushinagar (greenfield, correct), Vijayawada (brownfield, NOT greenfield) — trap caught students who assumed all three were greenfield.
traps.how_to_generate: List infrastructure projects. Include one that was recently upgraded/modernised but is actually old — that's the false greenfield claim.

traps.name: speaker_power_vs_president_power
traps.description: Assigns a power belonging to the Speaker (anti-defection, disqualification) to the President or Vice President.
traps.mechanism: Students know President has many powers and conflate constitutional roles.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2025: 'If any question arises as to whether a Member has become subject to disqualification under Tenth Schedule, the President's decision shall be final' — FALSE. It's the Speaker/Chairman who decides, not the President.
traps.how_to_generate: Take any Speaker/Chairman exclusive power. Assign it to President in a false statement. Common pairs: Speaker vs President, Speaker vs SC, Governor vs President.

traps.name: tenth_schedule_political_party_mention
traps.description: Claims 'political party' is NOT mentioned in the Constitution — it IS mentioned in the Tenth Schedule.
traps.mechanism: Students think 'political party' is a non-constitutional concept handled by RPA 1951.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2025: 'There is no mention of the word political party in the Constitution of India' — FALSE. Tenth Schedule explicitly uses the term.
traps.how_to_generate: Take a term students assume is outside the Constitution (coalition, political party, election symbol). One will actually be in the Constitution somewhere.

traps.name: money_bill_rajya_sabha_powers
traps.description: States Rajya Sabha can reject a Money Bill OR that its suggested amendments must be accepted by Lok Sabha — both are false.
traps.mechanism: Students know Rajya Sabha has limited powers on Money Bills but mix up exactly what it CAN and CANNOT do.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: Statement 3 — 'Rajya Sabha can either approve or suggest changes but cannot reject' — TRUE. Statement 4 — 'Amendments suggested by Rajya Sabha have to be accepted by Lok Sabha' — FALSE (Lok Sabha may or may not accept).
traps.how_to_generate: Use the exact wording from Constitution (Article 109, 110). Swap 'may accept' with 'must accept'. These qualifier flips are the core trap.

traps.name: schedule_wrong_part
traps.description: Assigns a constitutional provision to the wrong Part or Schedule number.
traps.mechanism: Students know what is in which Part but confuse Part IX/IX-A/XVIII/XX numbers.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: All three statements correct — Part IX-A (Municipalities), Part XVIII (Emergency), Part XX (Amendment). Trap was making students doubt one of them.
traps.how_to_generate: List 3 Part/Schedule numbers. Put 2 correct and 1 off by 1-2 (e.g., say Part XVII instead of XVIII for Emergency). OR make all 3 correct (answer = D) which students avoid.

traps.name: union_state_concurrent_list_wrong_placement
traps.description: Puts a subject in wrong list — e.g., Inter-State trade is Union List, but students think it's State or Concurrent.
traps.mechanism: Students know obvious items (defence = Union, police = State) but struggle with inter-State matters.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: 'Inter-State quarantine is a Union subject' — TRUE (correct answer C). Traps: Inter-State trade (actually Concurrent, not State), Inter-State migration (Concurrent, not State).
traps.how_to_generate: Pick 'Inter-State X' subjects. Students assume Inter-State anything = Union. Some are Concurrent. Use the wrong list in the false option.

traps.name: cds_command_vs_coordinate
traps.description: Says CDS exercises 'military command' over Service Chiefs — CDS coordinates, advises, but does NOT command.
traps.mechanism: Students assume the most senior military officer must have command authority.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: Statement 2 — 'CDS exercises military command over the three Service Chiefs' — FALSE. Correct duties: Permanent Chairman of Chiefs of Staff Committee (TRUE) + Principal Military Advisor to Defence Minister (TRUE).
traps.how_to_generate: Use roles that sound like command but are advisory (CDS, NSA, Cabinet Secretary). Insert 'command' in false statement, use 'coordinate/advise' in true one.

traps.name: nari_shakti_act_implementation_trigger
traps.description: States provisions come into effect from the 18th Lok Sabha — false. Requires delimitation first, which has not happened.
traps.mechanism: Students know Act was passed but don't know the implementation pre-condition (delimitation).
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: Statement 1 — 'Provisions will come into effect from the 18th Lok Sabha' — FALSE. Statement 2 — '15 years duration' — TRUE. Statement 3 — 'SC Women seats within SC quota' — TRUE.
traps.how_to_generate: For any recent constitutional amendment or Act, ask about implementation conditions (commencement date, pre-conditions). The 'when does it kick in' is always a trap.

traps.name: writ_wrong_issuing_authority_or_target
traps.description: Describes what a writ does but assigns it to wrong authority or wrong target body.
traps.mechanism: Students confuse Mandamus/Prohibition/Certiorari — all are writs but issued against different bodies for different purposes.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: Writ of Prohibition question — tests whether students know it's issued to inferior courts/tribunals to stop proceedings, not to government officers.
traps.how_to_generate: Take any writ (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Certiorari, Prohibition, Quo Warranto). State what a DIFFERENT writ does in the false option. Or say it can be issued against a body it CANNOT be issued against.

traps.name: ethics_committee_complaint_eligibility
traps.description: States non-MP can file complaint against MP to Ethics Committee — only an MP can file such a complaint.
traps.mechanism: Students assume any citizen can complain about MP conduct, like with Lokpal.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: Statement 2 — 'Only a Member of Lok Sabha can make a complaint about unethical conduct' — TRUE (this is the counterintuitive fact). Statement 3 — 'Cannot take up sub-judice matters' — TRUE.
traps.how_to_generate: For any parliamentary committee, ask about eligibility to file complaints, quorum rules, or what it cannot do. The restrictions are always the trap.

traps.name: lokpal_scope_exclusion
traps.description: States Lokpal cannot investigate PM, or that it covers Indian public servants posted abroad — both are tricky.
traps.mechanism: Lokpal CAN inquire into PM under certain conditions. It does NOT cover public servants posted outside India.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2025: Statement IV — 'Lokpal cannot inquire into allegations against sitting PM' — FALSE. Lokpal can under specific circumstances. Statement I — 'applies to public servants of India but not those posted outside' — TRUE.
traps.how_to_generate: Use any oversight institution (Lokpal, CVC, CAG). Ask about who it covers and who it excludes. Reverse a well-known exclusion.

traps.name: party_leader_wrong_match
traps.description: In match-the-pair, assigns a leader to the wrong political party — especially using founders vs prominent members.
traps.mechanism: Students know Rajagopalachari was prominent in Congress but forget he FOUNDED Swatantra Party. Narendra Dev is associated with Socialist movement but not the Swatantra Party.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: Swatantra Party — Acharya Narendra Dev (WRONG, should be C. Rajagopalachari). Socialist Party — C. Rajagopalachari (WRONG, should be Acharya Narendra Dev / Jayaprakash Narayan).
traps.how_to_generate: Match 4 parties/movements to 4 leaders. Put 2 correct and 2 crossed (leader A matched with party B and vice versa). Use leaders who overlap across ideological movements.

traps.name: buddhist_text_author_swap
traps.description: Assigns a Buddhist/Jain/Ancient text to the wrong author or tradition.
traps.mechanism: Students know text names but not the specific sect, author, or language they belong to.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: Works attributed to playwright Bhasa — Madhyama-vyayoga (correct). Kavyalankara (Bhamaha), Natyashastra (Bharata), Mahabhashya (Patanjali) — all real texts by different authors.
traps.how_to_generate: Pick any Sanskrit text or classical work. Give 4 real text names but only one is correctly attributed to the person in the question. Others are real texts by real but different authors.

traps.name: constituent_assembly_president_first_vs_later
traps.description: Confuses the Provisional President with the eventual President of Constituent Assembly — or confuses with Drafting Committee Chair.
traps.mechanism: Students know Dr. Rajendra Prasad was President of Constituent Assembly and B.R. Ambedkar chaired Drafting Committee. The Provisional President (Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha) is almost always unknown.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: 'Who was Provisional President before Rajendra Prasad?' — Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha. Common wrong answers: Rajagopalachari, Ambedkar, T.T. Krishnamachari.
traps.how_to_generate: Ask about 'first' or 'provisional' holders of roles that later became associated with more famous people. Use the famous name as a distractor.

traps.name: government_of_india_act_provision_reversal
traps.description: States a provision of GOI Act 1935 incorrectly — e.g., says defence/foreign affairs were under federal legislature when they were reserved for Governor-General.
traps.mechanism: Students know GOI 1935 had federation and residuary powers but get confused on what was 'reserved' vs 'transferred'.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: Statement 1 (All-India Federation with provinces and princely states) — TRUE. Statement 2 (Defence and Foreign Affairs under federal legislature) — FALSE. These were reserved subjects under Governor-General.
traps.how_to_generate: Pick any colonial legislation (GOI 1919, 1935, Rowlatt Act). State 2 provisions, one of which misassigns who controlled a key subject.

traps.name: ryotwari_zamindari_feature_swap
traps.description: Assigns a feature of Zamindari to Ryotwari or vice versa — especially regarding exemptions for bad harvest.
traps.mechanism: Students mix up the two settlement systems. Ryotwari had direct settlement with ryots, Zamindari had intermediaries.
traps.real_pyq_example: PYQ: 'Under Ryotwari Settlement, peasants were exempted from revenue payment in case of bad harvests' — this is actually a nuanced TRUE. The trap is students think only Zamindari had exemptions.
traps.how_to_generate: State a feature of one revenue settlement system and attribute it to the other. Or use a feature that sounds like it belongs to the more 'exploitative' system but actually belongs to the supposedly 'better' one.

traps.name: buddhist_monk_text_tradition_wrong
traps.description: Names an Indian Buddhist monk and asks which text they wrote — confuses Theravada/Mahayana/Sarvastivada traditions.
traps.mechanism: Students know major Buddhist texts (Prajnaparamita, Visuddhimagga) but cannot match them to specific monks and schools.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: Sanghabhuti — wrote commentary on Sarvastivada Vinaya. Distractors: Prajnaparamita Sutra (Mahayana), Visuddhimagga (Theravada), Lalitavistara (Mahayana biography of Buddha).
traps.how_to_generate: Name an obscure monk/scholar. Distractors = real texts from other traditions. Correct answer = the matching tradition's text.

traps.name: unesco_heritage_year_wrong
traps.description: Lists UNESCO World Heritage sites and asks which were added in a specific year — students confuse recent vs older listings.
traps.mechanism: Students know which sites ARE on the list but not the exact year of inscription.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: Shantiniketan and Sacred Ensembles of Hoysalas were added in 2023 (answer = 2). Rani-ki-Vav (2014) and Mahabodhi Temple (2002) are old listings used as distractors.
traps.how_to_generate: Mix 2-3 recent inscriptions with 1-2 older well-known ones. Ask 'how many were added in year X'. Answer is never 'all four'.

traps.name: exercise_military_wrong_country
traps.description: Names a bilateral military exercise and assigns it to the wrong country pair.
traps.mechanism: Students know exercise names but mix up which two countries participate, especially India-Sri Lanka vs India-Bangladesh vs India-Nepal.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: Exercise Mitra Shakti 2023 — Statement 1 'between India and Bangladesh' — FALSE. It is India-Sri Lanka. Commenced at Aundh, Pune (TRUE). Counter-terrorism goal (TRUE). IAF part (TRUE).
traps.how_to_generate: Name any bilateral exercise (Mitra Shakti, Shakti, Yudh Abhyas, SLINEX). State the partner country wrong. India's south Asian neighbours are interchangeable in student memory.

traps.name: frbm_debt_ratio_component_swap
traps.description: Gives FRBM target debt-to-GDP ratio but swaps the Centre vs States component.
traps.mechanism: Students know the total is 60% but flip Centre (40%) and States (20%) shares.
traps.real_pyq_example: PYQ: 'FRBM Review Committee recommended debt/GDP of 60% comprising 40% Centre + 20% States' — TRUE. Statement 2: 'Central Govt has domestic liabilities of 21% vs States' 49%' — FALSE. Actual: Centre has higher domestic debt than states.
traps.how_to_generate: Use any two-component fiscal target (Centre/State, direct/indirect tax, domestic/external debt). Swap the magnitudes between components.

traps.name: most_inflationary_policy_wrong_ranking
traps.description: Asks which policy is MOST inflationary — students confuse deficit monetisation with bank borrowing.
traps.mechanism: All four options are inflationary to some degree. Students must rank correctly: money creation > bank borrowing > public borrowing > debt repayment.
traps.real_pyq_example: PYQ: 'Which is likely MOST inflationary?' — Creation of new money to finance deficit (answer D). Students pick 'borrowing from banks' thinking it's the worst. Repayment of public debt is actually deflationary.
traps.how_to_generate: Use superlatives (most inflationary, least deflationary, most likely to cause crowding out). Options are all plausible economic mechanisms, ranked by students incorrectly.

traps.name: black_money_primary_harm_wrong
traps.description: Asks what is the PRIMARY harm of black money — students think corruption/politics, correct answer is tax revenue loss.
traps.mechanism: Students associate black money with political corruption and social harm, but the economic primary harm is fiscal: lost tax revenue.
traps.real_pyq_example: PYQ: Primary harm of black money — 'Loss of revenue to State Exchequer due to tax evasion' (answer D). Distractors: real estate diversion, luxury goods, political donations — all real effects but secondary.
traps.how_to_generate: Ask for PRIMARY/MOST SIGNIFICANT harm or cause when multiple effects are real. The institutionally/economically defined primary cause is always different from the socially visible one.

traps.name: interest_coverage_ratio_wrong_use
traps.description: States Interest Coverage Ratio measures present risk of a firm — it actually measures EMERGING/FUTURE risk in Indian banking context.
traps.mechanism: The standard definition says ICR measures ability to pay interest (present). But UPSC framed it as 'evaluating emerging risk' — which is the banking context interpretation.
traps.real_pyq_example: PYQ: ICR helps in 'evaluating the emerging risk of a firm that a bank is going to give a loan to' — correct in UPSC's answer. 'Present risk' framing marked as incorrect.
traps.how_to_generate: Use financial ratios (ICR, current ratio, debt-equity ratio). Ask what the ratio 'helps understand' and distinguish present vs emerging vs historical risk.

traps.name: edible_oil_import_vs_production
traps.description: States India imports more edible oil than it produces — TRUE — and that no customs duty is levied — FALSE (duty exists but is reduced).
traps.mechanism: India IS import dependent for edible oils. But government DOES levy customs duty (sometimes zero/reduced but not 'no duty at all').
traps.real_pyq_example: PYQ: Statement 1 (quantity imported > domestic production) — TRUE. Statement 2 (no customs duty on imported edible oils) — FALSE. This tests whether students confuse 'nil duty' periods with 'no duty policy'.
traps.how_to_generate: Pick any commodity where India is import-dependent. Statement 1: import level (true). Statement 2: policy claim about tariff (use absolute 'never' or 'always' which makes it false).

traps.name: state_loan_consent_condition
traps.description: States any State requires Centre's consent for raising loans — actually only states that ALREADY OWE outstanding loans to Centre.
traps.mechanism: Students think Centre has general power to approve state borrowings. It only applies when there's an outstanding liability.
traps.real_pyq_example: PYQ: 'As per Constitution, it is mandatory for a State to take Central Government consent for raising any loan if the former owes any outstanding liabilities to the latter' — TRUE (Statement 3). The condition (outstanding liabilities) is the trap — students think it's unconditional.
traps.how_to_generate: State any constitutional power with a CONDITION. Remove the condition in the false version. The conditionality is always what makes the true answer correct.

traps.name: low_cloud_warming_vs_cooling_effect
traps.description: States low clouds cause a COOLING effect — they actually cause WARMING by absorbing infrared radiation from Earth.
traps.mechanism: Students know high clouds (cirrus) cool by reflecting sunlight. They assume all clouds cool. Low clouds trap outgoing radiation = warming.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: 'Low clouds have high absorption of infrared radiation from Earth's surface and thus cause a warming effect' — TRUE. Students who assumed clouds always cool marked this wrong.
traps.how_to_generate: Use cloud types (high/low/middle) and assign wrong radiation effects (reflection vs absorption, solar vs terrestrial radiation).

traps.name: congo_basin_carbon_sink_lung_confusion
traps.description: Tests whether students know Congo Basin (not Amazon) is the world's largest carbon sink.
traps.mechanism: Amazon is called 'lungs of the Earth' in popular media. Congo Basin is actually the largest net carbon sink per scientific measurements.
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: DRC / Congo Basin — 'known as lungs of Africa, largest carbon sink in world, absorbing more carbon than Amazon' — correct per UPSC's answer.
traps.how_to_generate: Ask about superlatives for carbon sinks, biodiversity hotspots, or forest cover using either Amazon or Congo. Students will default to Amazon for most superlatives.

traps.name: cobalt_mining_byproduct_wrong
traps.description: States cobalt is primarily mined as a standalone mineral — it's actually a BYPRODUCT of copper and nickel mining.
traps.mechanism: Students know cobalt is used in batteries and DRC is the main producer, but don't know the extraction method (byproduct, not primary mine).
traps.real_pyq_example: 2024: 'Cobalt is primarily mined as a byproduct of nickel and copper mining' — TRUE. Students who thought cobalt has dedicated mines marked this wrong.
traps.how_to_generate: Use any strategic/critical mineral (cobalt, lithium, rare earths). Ask about primary vs byproduct extraction. Many critical minerals are byproducts.

traps.name: ramsar_wetland_criteria_wrong
traps.description: States a specific criterion for Ramsar designation that is slightly wrong — especially the 20,000 waterbird threshold.
traps.mechanism: Students know Ramsar is about wetlands but not the exact criteria numbers and conditions.
traps.real_pyq_example: Recurring PYQ type: 'A wetland qualifies for Ramsar listing if it regularly supports 20,000 waterfowl' — this IS one of the criteria but students mark it wrong because they think it's arbitrary.
traps.how_to_generate: State the actual numerical criteria with a slight modification (10,000 instead of 20,000, 1% instead of actual threshold). Or swap Ramsar criteria with IUCN criteria.

traps.name: treaty_body_wrong_secretariat
traps.description: Assigns the secretariat of an environmental convention to the wrong city/organisation.
traps.mechanism: CITES (Geneva), CBD (Montreal), UNFCCC (Bonn), Ramsar (Gland, Switzerland) — students mix up host cities.
traps.real_pyq_example: Recurring: 'CITES secretariat is located in' — options include Geneva, Nairobi, Montreal, Bonn. Students confuse with UNEP (Nairobi) or IPCC (Geneva).
traps.how_to_generate: Match environmental conventions to their secretariat cities. Include two that are in the same city or same country to increase confusion.

traps.name: ozone_vs_greenhouse_gas_confusion
traps.description: Claims ozone IS a greenhouse gas — it IS, but students think it's not because its main role is UV protection.
traps.mechanism: Students learn about ozone for UV protection and never connect it to greenhouse warming. But ozone IS a greenhouse gas in the troposphere.
traps.real_pyq_example: PYQ multi-statement type: 'Tropospheric ozone is a greenhouse gas' — TRUE. 'Stratospheric ozone is a greenhouse gas' — also technically true but less impactful. Students mark both wrong.
traps.how_to_generate: Use any gas that has dual or unexpected roles (ozone, water vapor, methane vs CO2 comparison by GWP). Ask about its classification in a way that requires knowing the secondary role.

traps.name: isro_mission_wrong_objective
traps.description: Assigns the wrong primary objective to an ISRO mission — e.g., says Chandrayaan-3 targeted equatorial region vs south pole.
traps.mechanism: Students know mission names but not precise landing sites, instruments, or primary objectives.
traps.real_pyq_example: Pattern: 'Chandrayaan-3 landed near the lunar equator' — FALSE. It landed near the south pole (first mission to do so). Distractors include equatorial region and dark side of Moon.
traps.how_to_generate: Name any ISRO/DRDO mission. Give 3-4 statements about objectives/payloads/launch vehicles. Mix one wrong one (wrong orbit, wrong instrument, wrong objective).

traps.name: semiconductor_property_wrong
traps.description: States that semiconductor conductivity increases with temperature — TRUE, opposite of metals — students assume it behaves like metals.
traps.mechanism: Students know semiconductors are between conductors and insulators but assume conductivity goes down with heat like metals.
traps.real_pyq_example: PYQ type: 'Conductivity of semiconductors increases with rise in temperature' — TRUE. This is counterintuitive to students who compare with metals.
traps.how_to_generate: Use any physical property where semiconductors behave opposite to metals (conductivity, resistance, band gap). State the semiconductor property; students apply metal logic.

traps.name: mRNA_vaccine_dna_integration_false
traps.description: States mRNA vaccines alter human DNA — FALSE. They use mRNA which does not enter cell nucleus and cannot integrate into DNA.
traps.mechanism: Students fear or believe the popular misconception that mRNA vaccines change genetic code.
traps.real_pyq_example: PYQ 2022 type: 'mRNA vaccines alter the genetic structure of the host' — FALSE. The mRNA degrades after producing spike protein and never touches nuclear DNA.
traps.how_to_generate: For any new technology (mRNA, CRISPR, nanotechnology), state the most common public misconception as a false statement. The correct science is the trap against the misconception.

traps.name: ai_ml_dl_wrong_hierarchy
traps.description: States AI is a subset of ML, or that DL and ML are the same — correct hierarchy is AI ⊃ ML ⊃ DL.
traps.mechanism: Students confuse the relationship direction. AI is the broadest, ML is a type of AI, Deep Learning is a type of ML.
traps.real_pyq_example: PYQ type: 'Machine Learning is a subset of Artificial Intelligence' — TRUE. 'Deep Learning is a subset of Machine Learning' — TRUE. Trap: 'Artificial Intelligence is a subset of Machine Learning' — FALSE.
traps.how_to_generate: Draw the correct hierarchy (AI > ML > DL > NN). Swap the subset direction in one false statement. Use 'is a part of' vs 'contains' language.

traps.name: 5g_frequency_band_wrong
traps.description: States 5G operates on lower frequencies than 4G — FALSE. 5G uses higher frequency (mmWave) bands for speed, though it also uses sub-6GHz.
traps.mechanism: Students know 5G is faster but assume higher speed = lower frequency (like comparing AM/FM radio). Actually higher frequency = higher speed but lower range.
traps.real_pyq_example: PYQ type: 'Unlike 4G, 5G technology uses higher frequency radio waves' — TRUE. 'Higher frequency means better range' — FALSE (higher frequency = shorter range, more towers needed).
traps.how_to_generate: Use any connectivity technology (5G, satellite internet, WiFi bands). Test the frequency-speed-range relationship — students always confuse at least one of these.

traps.name: quantum_entanglement_communication_speed
traps.description: States quantum entanglement allows faster-than-light communication — FALSE. Entanglement is real but cannot be used to transmit information faster than light.
traps.mechanism: Popular science presents entanglement as 'spooky action at a distance' which sounds like instant communication.
traps.real_pyq_example: PYQ type: 'Quantum entanglement can be used to transmit information faster than the speed of light' — FALSE. Entanglement allows correlated measurements but not information transfer.
traps.how_to_generate: Use any quantum technology concept (entanglement, superposition, quantum computing). State the popular misconception as a false statement.
